newsitem.title: INDIA: Rail freight hike seen hurting India firms.
newsitem.headline: Rail freight hike seen hurting India firms.

text.p: A 12 percent freight hike announced by Indian Railways on Wednesday would raise costs and squeeze the margins of most sections of Indian industry, producers and analysts said.
It would hurt manufacturers of commodity products such as steel, cement and plastics most, they said.
Mukesh Gupta, director of Lloyds Steel Industries said steel prices would go up by about 150 rupees per tonne following the rail freight increase.
"It won't affect us much because we move only eight to 10 percent by rail," Gupta told Reuters. "It will hasten the shift from rail to road transportation," he said.

Indian Railway Minister Ram Vilas Paswan, presenting the railway budget for 1997/98 (April-March) on Wednesday, announced a 12 percent hike in freight rates of all goods except 15 items including grains, sugar, fuel and fertilisers.
Stockbrokers said the rise was in line with expectations.
"The market was expecting a hike of 12 to 15 percent. So this has little impact on stocks," Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at brokerage Kotak Securities.

"It would push up prices of most goods," said Anil Singhvi, treasurer at Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd, a leading cement maker. He said most industry officials had been expecting an 8.0-10.0 percent freight hike.
"What is worse, the industry won't be able to pass on the higher costs as demand is on the lower side," he told Reuters.
"It will affect corporate bottomlines," Singhvi said.
An official of Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO), India's largest private steel maker, said the new rates would raise costs but "it is too early to say by how much".
He said over 60 percent of India's steel production is transported by rail.
Dinshaw Irani, head of research at Lloyds Securities, said cement firms will be hit from both sides -- raw materials such as coal on the one side as well as end products moving by rail.
"The way the demand is, they won't be able to pass on the higher costs," Irani said.

Exporters said they found little cheer in the railway budget. "They have exempted foodgrains and the like," said N.K. Goyal, chairman of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO) and a leading garment exporter.
"What's left is commodities that are exported," he said.
The budget would not help Indian exports which have been slowing down in recent months because of increasing cost of production and an overvalued rupee, Goyal said.
The new freight rates take effect from April and are expected to fetch the exchequer 18.0 billion rupees.
The rail budget also set a freight target of 430 million rupees compared with 410 million rupees a year earlier.
India's main 1997/98 budget will be presented to parliament on Friday by the Finance Minister P. Chidambaram.
